title: A shelf-stable oxygen carrier that can replace donor red cells in hemorrhage

concept.text: The proposed innovation is an oxygen-carrying product that can be stored without refrigeration and administered during life-threatening bleeding to perform the oxygen-delivery function of donor red cells. It would need to work at the volumes and repeat doses that resuscitation requires, with acceptable safety, and without blood-type matching. The target is a clinically effective replacement for red-cell oxygen delivery when donor blood is unavailable or delayed; the supplied evidence does not establish that this combined capability has been achieved.

Hemoglobin-based oxygen carriers are a major route toward this goal. Hemoglobin normally carries oxygen inside red cells, but earlier products using purified hemoglobin outside those cells encountered serious toxicity. Researchers have explored chemical cross-linking, polymerization, lipid encapsulation, and recombinant modification to improve performance. These approaches are documented in the supplied review's abstract and retained figure-caption text, but their exploration does not establish that any design meets the full clinical and storage requirements.

Scope clarification: replacing red-cell oxygen delivery is narrower than replacing whole blood. An oxygen carrier would not itself seal a bleeding vessel, supply platelets or clotting factors, or remove the need for surgery and other bleeding-control measures. The concept belongs primarily to emergency clinical medicine, with enabling work in protein engineering, biomaterials, and pharmaceutical formulation.

significance.text: Donor-dependent transfusion has substantial logistical constraints. The supplied review identifies reliance on volunteer donors, supply shortages, short storage life, possible infectious transmission, and immune complications, with many limitations more severe in low-income countries. These constraints explain why a safe alternative could matter even where donor red cells are already effective when available promptly.

Conditional impact assessment: a safe, shelf-stable product that requires no type matching could make oxygen delivery available closer to the point of bleeding, including during transport or in facilities with limited blood-banking capacity. Its revolutionary feature would be access and deployment: preserving a resuscitation option when donor red cells cannot arrive in time. That impact depends on demonstrated efficacy, storage reliability, sufficient supply, and practical administration, rather than on oxygen-carrying capacity alone.

Potential downstream uses include trauma care, obstetric hemorrhage, and remote or resource-constrained emergency care. These are plausible applications, not established benefits across those populations. Use by patients who refuse donor blood would also depend on the product's composition and individual acceptance. A successful carrier could complement bleeding control and coagulation support, but it would not make them unnecessary or establish superiority over promptly available donor red cells.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability is the combination of useful oxygen delivery, acceptable safety at resuscitation doses, and shelf stability. The review describes hypertension caused by vasoconstriction and multiple organ toxicities with early purified native hemoglobin. It attributes these effects partly to nitric-oxide scavenging, reactive oxygen species, and possible sterile inflammation. Later large clinical trials continued to encounter elevated adverse-event rates, failure to meet specified clinical endpoints, or both.

Engineering synthesis: a candidate must carry and release enough oxygen to improve tissue oxygenation while avoiding effects on vascular tone and organ function that undermine that benefit. Chemical modification, polymerization, encapsulation, and recombinant redesign offer different ways to alter hemoglobin's behavior, but the supplied evidence does not establish which approach, if any, resolves the clinical tradeoffs. Repeated administration and clinically necessary volumes are requirements to test, not dose-specific capabilities demonstrated by this record.

Engineering synthesis: storage must preserve both oxygen-delivery performance and safety throughout a specified unrefrigerated shelf life. Success therefore requires more than a promising freshly manufactured formulation: manufacture, storage, transport, and administration must yield a consistent product. Whether encapsulated hemoglobin or a design outside the cell-free hemoglobin approach can avoid earlier toxicities remains unresolved by the supplied evidence; those earlier failures do not prove that every alternative must fail.

current_state.text: The sole supplied scientific source is Youmna Abdelghany and colleagues' review, “Artificial Oxygen Carriers: Lessons From Hemoglobin-Based Oxygen Carrier Clinical Trials and Current Development Efforts,” published online on September 12, 2025, and in the March 1, 2026 issue of Shock, volume 65(3), pages 374–389. It summarizes decades of development of cell-free hemoglobin products as potential substitutes for red-cell transfusion. It reports promising preliminary findings alongside large clinical trials with elevated adverse events and/or failure to meet specified endpoints. This supports continued investigation and a substantial unresolved safety-and-efficacy barrier, rather than an achieved replacement capability.

The review reports that no hemoglobin-based oxygen carrier had obtained US Food and Drug Administration approval for clinical use. This is a statement in the review's publication context, not an independently verified regulatory update through November 2026. Its retained Figure 2 caption documents cross-linking, polymerization, lipid encapsulation, and recombinant modification as development approaches; the supplied review does not establish that any one approach has demonstrated the complete capability described here.

The available evidence is the supplied PubMed record, including its abstract, retained figure captions, and conflict-of-interest disclosures. The full review and figure images were not inspected in the supplied assessment. Several authors disclose relevant commercial roles, shareholdings, or patents involving heme-based therapeutics and artificial oxygen carriers. These disclosures provide context for interpreting the review; they do not by themselves invalidate its findings.

The retained PubMed record exposes only a subset of the review's 187 references. It therefore does not verify the earlier assertion that this review cites a particular 2008 meta-analysis of death and myocardial infarction, and no risk ratios from that analysis can be carried forward from the supplied evidence. The reference-display limitation is not evidence that the full review omits the analysis. Foreign licensure and named expanded-access products also remain unverified here.

Evidence boundary: the source was retrieved on November 1, 2026, but retrieval of an older review does not establish coverage of developments up to that date. No freshness-search record was supplied. The materials consequently leave subsequent trials, regulatory changes, and the present performance of alternative designs unassessed; this gap does not contradict the review's dated clinical summary.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed clinical demonstration: randomized trials in life-threatening hemorrhage, in settings where immediate donor red cells are limited or delayed, should show that the product supports survival and reversal of shock at least as well as the available standard. Trial designs should specify clinically justified efficacy and safety margins in advance and assess death, myocardial infarction, and severe organ injury. These are proposed criteria for this concept, not established standards endorsed by the supplied review.
completion_criteria.label: Randomized trials demonstrate comparable hemorrhage survival and shock reversal

completion_criteria.text: Proposed dosing and storage demonstration: the product should remain effective and acceptably safe at clinically necessary volumes and repeat doses, rather than only after a small initial exposure. It should have a validated shelf life under explicitly specified conditions that do not require refrigeration, with retained performance and safety through the claimed storage period. Administration without type matching should be demonstrated within a clearly defined intended-use population.
completion_criteria.label: Effective resuscitation dosing with validated unrefrigerated storage and unmatched administration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: convincing evidence should extend across manufacturing lots, clinical sites, and representative patients, with transparent reporting of adverse events, concurrent resuscitation treatments, and circumstances in which the product fails or should not be used. Evidence from one hemorrhage setting should not automatically be generalized to trauma, obstetric bleeding, every age group, or all comorbidities. Finite trials can establish demonstrated breadth within those boundaries, not literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Reproducible clinical evidence with reported harms and applicability limits

completion_criteria.text: Proposed scope threshold: veterinary approval, individual-patient expanded access, improved laboratory oxygen measurements, or preliminary safety findings alone would not demonstrate replacement of donor red-cell oxygen delivery in life-threatening human hemorrhage. Clinical benefit must be shown alongside the storage and administration capabilities. Bleeding control and coagulation support remain part of care even if the oxygen carrier succeeds.
completion_criteria.label: Human hemorrhage benefit demonstrated alongside storage and administration capabilities

related_concepts.text: Conceptual comparison with the supplied roster: CLM-05, “Durable organ xenotransplantation at clinical scale,” and CLM-11, “Implantable human-scale organs assembled outside the body,” share the aim of reducing dependence on scarce donated biological resources. CLM-14 instead seeks an acutely administered oxygen-delivery product. It does not require a living organ to integrate and function durably after implantation, so their clinical endpoints and engineering barriers remain distinct.

Conceptual comparison: CLM-06, “Therapeutic remuscularization of the adult human heart,” and CLM-15, “Restoration of nephron number in the adult human kidney,” address lasting tissue restoration. CLM-14 seeks temporary physiological support during an emergency. Avoiding cardiac and renal injury is an important safety requirement for an oxygen carrier, but delivering oxygen or avoiding injury does not itself regenerate heart muscle or nephrons.

Conceptual comparison: CLM-01, “Programmable antigen-specific immune tolerance,” overlaps with the broad concern of immune compatibility. However, giving an oxygen carrier without blood-type matching would not establish programmed immune tolerance or eliminate every possible immune reaction. CLM-09, “Curative in vivo genome writing beyond the liver,” shares a broad connection to molecular engineering, but recombinant redesign of a manufactured carrier is distinct from editing a patient's genome. These roster entries retain separate identities and completion criteria.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not identify a product that meets the combined hemorrhage-efficacy, safety, dosing, type-matching, and unrefrigerated-storage requirements.
Regulatory status and clinical developments after the review's publication context remain unassessed; foreign licensure and named expanded-access products are not verified.
The full review, figure images, and complete reference list were not inspected in the supplied assessment. The claimed 2008 meta-analysis citation and its quantitative results remain unverified.
It remains unresolved whether a particular modified, encapsulated, or alternative oxygen-carrier design can avoid earlier toxicities at clinically necessary volumes and repeat doses.

Specific shelf-life duration, storage-temperature range, dosing regimen, trial margins, and intended-use populations require product-specific justification; none is established by the supplied materials.

brief.title: An oxygen-carrying substitute for donor red blood cells
possible: Someone bleeding heavily could receive an oxygen-carrying fluid when donor red blood cells cannot arrive in time. It could be kept without refrigeration and given without matching blood types, including at the large volumes and repeated doses needed during emergency care.
why: Ambulance crews and hospitals with limited blood supplies could keep oxygen delivery within reach. This could help people with severe injuries or bleeding during childbirth, especially where blood banks are scarce.

sources.showed: Their review describes efforts to use hemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying protein in red cells, outside those cells. Early products caused high blood pressure and organ damage; larger trials continued to find harm or missed treatment goals.
sources.quote: Despite some promising results in preliminary studies, large-scale clinical trials have continued to show elevated rates of adverse events and/or a failure to meet specified clinical endpoints.
sources.cited_for: Past human trials expose the central challenge of delivering oxygen without causing serious harm.
sources.not_established: The review does not establish a safe, effective replacement that also meets the dosing and storage requirements.

sources.who: Masahiro Tokuno, Kazuaki Taguchi and colleagues
sources.showed: In rats with severe blood loss, stored hemoglobin enclosed in tiny fat membranes supported recovery comparably to fresh red cells, without the lung injury associated with older stored red cells.
sources.quote: The six-hour mortality after resuscitation was not significantly different among the groups.
sources.cited_for: Stored carriers retained useful oxygen-delivery performance in an animal experiment.
sources.not_established: An animal experiment does not establish survival benefit or safety at the volumes and repeated doses needed in people.

sources.showed: In a small dog study, membrane-enclosed hemoglobin restored blood pressure and oxygen delivery after severe bleeding following removal of a lung. It performed better than a protein fluid without the carrier.
sources.quote:
Oxygen delivery was restored in the HbV group 
and was significantly higher than that in the HSA group (P < 0.0001).
sources.cited_for: The carrier supported oxygen delivery despite blood loss and reduced lung function.
sources.not_established: This small animal study did not establish benefit in human bleeding or equivalence to donor red cells.

shown: Tokuno and colleagues found that a carrier stored for a year supported recovery after severe bleeding in rats comparably to fresh red cells. Nakano and colleagues restored oxygen delivery in dogs after lung removal and blood loss. Human trials of earlier hemoglobin products have faced serious safety problems.
missing: Human trials have yet to establish comparable survival and recovery with acceptable risks of heart attack and severe organ injury.
A product must combine safe emergency volumes and repeated doses with proven unrefrigerated storage and use without blood-type matching.
Reliable results must extend across production batches, hospitals and clearly defined patient groups.

milestones.label: Comparable survival and recovery after severe bleeding
milestones.explanation: Randomized trials would have to show comparable survival and reversal of shock, when circulation cannot meet the body's needs, with acceptable harm. This would establish benefit when donor red cells are delayed.

milestones.label: Effective repeated dosing after storage without refrigeration
milestones.explanation: The carrier would have to remain effective and acceptably safe at emergency volumes and repeat doses after its claimed unrefrigerated shelf life, without blood-type matching. This would establish practical emergency use.

milestones.label: Repeatable clinical results with clear limits and harms
milestones.explanation: Results would have to hold across production batches, hospitals and representative patients, with harms, accompanying treatments and failures reported. This would define whom the carrier can reliably help.

milestones.label: Human benefit combined with storage and administration capabilities
milestones.explanation: Human bleeding trials would have to demonstrate benefit alongside storage and administration capabilities. This would establish replacement of red-cell oxygen delivery; bleeding control and support for clotting would remain necessary.

uncertain: It remains unclear which carrier design can avoid earlier toxic effects at the volumes and repeated doses needed during severe bleeding.
Storage conditions, shelf life, dosing and acceptable trial margins need justification for each product.
Benefits in one bleeding setting may not extend to childbirth, other ages or people with other illnesses.

page.title: Shelf-stable oxygen therapeutics for hemorrhage
page.definition: An oxygen therapeutic, a fluid that transports oxygen in place of donor red cells, supports resuscitation from life-threatening hemorrhage without blood-group matching. Its validated storage conditions require no refrigeration, and its approved dose regimen supplies the oxygen-delivery function needed during treatment.

goal.need: US dating periods for red cells in additive solutions are 42 days at 1–6°C. DARPA identifies cold-chain storage and limited shelf life as barriers to delivering blood before hospital care. An unrefrigerated oxygen therapeutic would address the oxygen-delivery part of that problem when donor red cells are unavailable.

figures.caption: US dating periods for refrigerated red cells
figures.note: Periods run from collection. Approved or cleared collection, processing and storage system instructions may specify different periods.

statements.body: DARPA, Resuscitation and Prevention of Ischemia-Induced Dysfunction (RAPIID) programme
statements.quote: RAPIID will advance synthetic, shelf-stable blood components through clinical trials, regulatory approval, manufacturing scale-up, and the development of ruggedized fielding technologies.
statements.context: The programme includes stand-alone oxygen carriers alongside platelet products and dried plasma.

statements.quote: In turn, this would enable scientists to pick and choose among various biochemical characteristics to support the design of safe and effective products.
statements.context: FDA describes the purpose of comparing hemoglobin-based oxygen carriers that had failed clinical studies because of toxicity.

completion.title: An oxygen therapeutic gains FDA approval for hemorrhage with unrefrigerated storage.
completion.criterion: FDA approves or licenses an oxygen therapeutic for oxygen-delivery support during life-threatening human hemorrhage when donor red cells are unavailable. The approved indication, administration instructions and stability-supported labeling must cover use without blood-group matching and storage without refrigeration. The approved dose and any repeat dosing define the demonstrated replacement capacity; storage temperature and expiry remain product-specific.
completion.set_by: US Department of Health and Human Services/BARDA, Integrated Technology Readiness Levels for Medical Countermeasure Products, criterion 8C; applied to the indication and storage capability defined here.
completion.basis: HHS uses approval or licensure as its authorization threshold and requires stability studies supporting labeled expiry. Applying that test to this indication avoids inventing a universal dose or storage duration. The March 2026 review reports no FDA-approved hemoglobin-based oxygen carrier. FDA withdrew its oxygen-therapeutics draft guidance on 8 May 2015; that document supplies no current regulatory threshold.

milestones.title: An oxygen therapeutic demonstrates preliminary efficacy in a living-animal hemorrhage model.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate preliminary efficacy in living animals, corresponding to HHS TRL 3. On 31 October 2016, Tokuno et al. reported similar six-hour mortality after hemorrhagic shock with HbV stored for one year at 4°C (n=11) and fresh red cells (n=12); absence of a significant difference does not establish equivalence. On 22 March 2024, Nakano et al. reported restored oxygen delivery after removal of one lung and 30% blood-volume loss in dogs: HbV versus albumin, n=4 per group, P<0.0001.
milestones.set_by: HHS/BARDA, Integrated Technology Readiness Levels, TRL 3. HbV denotes hemoglobin enclosed in lipid vesicles.

milestones.title: An oxygen carrier meets RAPIID’s 10% performance margin and six-month storage test.
milestones.criterion: Meet RAPIID’s preclinical tests: safety and efficacy within a 10% margin of the comparable blood component; non-toxicity and pharmacological safety in IND-enabling assessments; and at least six months’ storage at sustained 4°C, 25°C and 40°C with no more than 10% change in physicochemical characteristics and functionality versus composition-matched unstored product. Government-chosen final packaging must additionally pass at least three months at those temperatures. These are programme metrics, not human clinical noninferiority margins.
milestones.set_by: DARPA, RAPIID solicitation DARPA-PS-26-124, Amendment 1, section 2.3.2.1 and Table 2; metrics for individual blood analog components.
milestones.threshold_quote: Demonstrate ≥6 months shelf-stability at 4, 25, and 40°C with ≤10% difference in physicochemical characteristics and functionality vs. fresh product

milestones.title: A regulator permits an oxygen therapeutic to enter a human clinical trial.
milestones.criterion: For the US route, an Investigational New Drug application is in effect 30 days after FDA receipt without a clinical hold, or earlier on FDA notification; ethics approval and other applicable protections also apply. Research using an exception from informed consent requires prior written FDA authorization. A Japanese precedent is HbV-101, approved by PMDA and Hokkaido University’s ethics committee before the first-in-human study that began in 2020.
milestones.set_by: FDA, 21 CFR 312.40 and 312.20(c), for the US route; Japan’s Pharmaceuticals and Medical Devices Agency approved the cited HbV-101 protocol.
milestones.threshold_quote: Thirty days after FDA receives the IND

milestones.title: An oxygen therapeutic completes an initial human safety and pharmacokinetic assessment.
milestones.criterion: Complete a phase 1 study establishing initial safety, pharmacokinetics and immunogenicity assessment as appropriate, the HHS TRL 6C test. The 2022 HbV report included 11 exposed healthy men: four at 10 mL, four at 50 mL and three assigned 100 mL. Two completed 100 mL; the third stopped after about 10 mL because of a rash. No serious adverse events occurred. A separate phase Ib protocol plans 16 participants and doses up to 400 mL; its registry said Not Recruiting on 23 October 2026, without efficacy results.
milestones.set_by: HHS/BARDA, Integrated Technology Readiness Levels, criterion 6C. The cited human studies concern encapsulated hemoglobin.
milestones.threshold_quote: establish an initial safety, pharmacokinetics and immunogenicity assessment as appropriate.

milestones.title: Controlled human studies establish an oxygen therapeutic’s preliminary efficacy and short-term risks.
milestones.criterion: Complete controlled studies evaluating efficacy for the hemorrhage indication and common short-term adverse effects, corresponding to FDA phase 2. In 1998, 44 trauma patients received PolyHeme (n=21; up to six units, 300 g hemoglobin) or red cells (n=23). Mean donor-red-cell use through day 1 was 6.8±3.9 versus 10.4±4.2 units, P<0.05. This blood-sparing result did not establish a survival benefit.
milestones.set_by: FDA, 21 CFR 312.21(b), definition of phase 2 investigations; the cited controlled study evaluated polymerized human hemoglobin.
milestones.threshold_quote: evaluate the effectiveness of the drug for a particular indication or indications

milestones.title: An oxygen carrier meets a pivotal hemorrhage trial’s prespecified 30-day mortality endpoint.
milestones.criterion: For the historical PolyHeme protocol, the upper confidence limit for excess 30-day mortality over control had to remain within seven percentage points; superiority was an alternative primary efficacy endpoint. Northfield’s 2008 filing reports failure in the primary modified intention-to-treat population: 714 randomized and treated patients, upper limit 7.65 percentage points. The per-protocol population passed, at 6.21 points, but did not rescue the failed primary analysis. This is a product-specific precedent, not a class-wide acceptable mortality margin.
milestones.set_by: Northfield Laboratories, PolyHeme phase III protocol and FDA Special Protocol Assessment, described in its 2008 Form 10-K; written for polymerized human hemoglobin.
milestones.threshold_quote: The margin to assess noninferiority, using the upper limit of the confidence interval, was set at 7% more than control.

not_found: No current FDA oxygen-therapeutic-specific guidance prescribing a universal human mortality margin or resuscitation dose was found.
No published result was found combining the RAPIID storage test with a successful pivotal human hemorrhage trial in one product.
No results report for the phase Ib study jRCT2051240249 was found.

results.finding: In hemorrhaged rats, 6-hour survival was 90.9% with stored HbV (n=11) versus 83.3% with fresh red cells (n=12).
results.detail: HbV was stored for one year at 4°C. The survival difference was not statistically significant; this does not establish equivalence.
results.quote: A higher 6-hour survival rate was found in the HbV group (90.9%). However, no significant difference was found among the groups.

results.finding: In hemorrhaged rats, 6-hour survival was 90.9% with stored HbV (n=11) versus 83.3% with fresh red cells (n=12).
results.detail: This comparative efficacy result does not establish performance within RAPIID’s 10% margin. The study also does not report the complete IND-enabling safety and specified storage and packaging tests.
results.quote: A higher 6-hour survival rate was found in the HbV group (90.9%). However, no significant difference was found among the groups.

results.finding: In dogs with hemorrhagic shock, HbV restored oxygen delivery versus albumin (n=4 per group; P < 0.0001).
results.detail: Dogs underwent pneumonectomy and approximately 30% blood-volume loss; oxygen delivery was compared over time after resuscitation.
results.quote:
Oxygen delivery was restored in the HbV group 
and was significantly higher than that in the HSA group (P < 0.0001).

results.finding: VS-101-treated rats (n=9) had 67% survival at eight hours after severe hemorrhagic shock.
results.detail: All three comparator groups had no survivors at eight hours. The randomized study was unblinded and assessed short-term outcomes in male rats.
results.quote:
Even compared with whole blood,
VS
-101 was the only group with survivors (67%) at the end of the 8-h observation period.

results.finding: In pigs with uncontrolled hemorrhagic shock, YQ23 increased oxygen delivery to 1.85 times the lactated Ringer’s control (n=6/group).
results.detail: The study also reported increased oxygen consumption. The pig groups were small; the authors noted that statistical significance for some indicators was unclear.

results.finding: In 11 healthy men exposed to hemoglobin vesicles, the estimated blood half-life was approximately 8 hours.
results.detail: Safety, pharmacokinetics and immune markers were assessed, but the final cohort was terminated before the fourth planned participant received a dose. Pharmacokinetic results were reported for two participants who completed the 100 mL infusion.
results.quote:
Pharmacokinetic analysis results revealed that HbVs circulate in the
bloodstream with a half-life of approximately 8 hours ( Figure 2 C).

results.finding: In 44 trauma patients, PolyHeme reduced mean donor-red-cell use through day 1 to 6.8 versus 10.4 units.
results.detail: The randomized phase 2 trial reported no serious or unexpected PolyHeme-related adverse events. The blood-sparing result did not establish a survival benefit.
results.quote: The total number of allogeneic red cell transfusions for the control and experimental groups was 10.4+/-4.2 units vs. 6.8+/-3.9 units (p < 0.05) through day 1, and 11.3+/-4.1 units vs. 7.8 +/-4.2 units (p = 0.06) through day 3.
